paragraphs.heading: A crystal's preferred breaks
paragraphs.text: Cleavage is the tendency of a crystalline material to split along definite planes set by its crystal structure. The flat breaks that result are themselves called cleavage. The planes are directions of relative weakness. They come from the regular positions that atoms and ions hold in the crystal, and these produce smooth repeating surfaces. These surfaces can be seen under a microscope and with the naked eye.

paragraphs.heading: Weak bonds decide
paragraphs.text: If the bonds in some directions are weaker than in others, the crystal tends to split along the weakly bonded planes. Every single crystal shows some tendency to split along the atomic planes of its structure. But when the differences between one direction and another are not large enough, the mineral does not display cleavage. Corundum is an example of a mineral with none.

paragraphs.heading: Diamond and graphite
paragraphs.text: Diamond and graphite are each made only of carbon. In diamond, every carbon atom is joined to four others in a tetrahedral pattern by short covalent bonds, and the cleavage planes run in four directions. In graphite, the carbon atoms sit in layers with a hexagonal pattern, and the covalent bonds there are shorter, and so even stronger, than diamond's. Each layer, though, is tied to the next by a van der Waals bond that is longer and much weaker. That gives graphite a single direction of cleavage. The weak bond breaks with little force, so the layers shear apart, graphite feels slippery, and it makes an excellent dry lubricant.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the planes
paragraphs.text: One cleavage plane gives basal cleavage, which is why thin sheets can be peeled off mica. Two planes, but not three, give prismatic cleavage. Three planes meeting at 90 degrees give cubic cleavage, so broken crystals of halite, or salt, form more cubes. Three planes meeting at other angles give rhombohedral cleavage, as in calcite. Four planes give octahedral cleavage, found in fluorite and diamond, and six planes give dodecahedral cleavage, found in sphalerite.

paragraphs.heading: Parting is not cleavage
paragraphs.text: Parting breaks look very similar to cleavage, but the cause is different. Cleavage comes from weakness in the crystal's basic design, while parting comes from growth defects, which are departures from that design. So cleavage occurs in every sample of a particular mineral, and parting only in samples with structural defects. Corundum, which has no cleavage, can show rhombohedral and basal parting.

paragraphs.heading: Putting cleavage to work
paragraphs.text: Cleavage is a physical property long used to identify minerals, both in hand-sized specimens and under the microscope. The angles between prismatic cleavage planes are diagnostic: 88–92° for the pyroxenes and 56–124° for the amphiboles. Cleavage also has technical importance in gemstone cutting and the electronics industry. Gem cutters generally cleave precious stones by impact, as is done in diamond cutting. Semiconductor materials made as synthetic single crystals are generally sold in thin wafers, which cleave much more easily.
